economies.name: United States
economies.profile:
The United States produced 26.00% of world GDP in 2025, holding 1st place of 196 economies with output of US$30.77 trillion, a rank it also held in 2000 and the IMF expects it to keep in 2030. Real growth ran at 2.2%, while US$ GDP rose 5.0% from US$29.30 trillion in 2024. China sits directly below it in 2nd.

As of 2021, services accounted for 76.3% of output, industry 17.6% and agriculture 0.9%, with manufacturing at 10.5%. GDP per capita reached US$90,027, 8th in the world, though the country ranks 12th on a purchasing-power basis. Inflation stood at 2.7% and unemployment at 4.2%, while government gross debt reached 124.4% of GDP. Output has grown 3.0 times in US$ terms since 2000, when it stood at US$10.25 trillion. The IMF projects GDP of US$38.60 trillion by 2030, a 25% increase.

economies.name: China

size_equivalent.label: Larger than any U.S. state (4.5× California)
size_equivalent.name: California

economies.profile:
China held 2nd place in 2025 with GDP of US$19.50 trillion, 16.48% of the world total and 15.9 times its 2000 level, when it ranked 6th. Real growth ran at +5.0%, while US$ GDP rose 4.1% from US$18.73 trillion. Consumer prices barely moved, with inflation at 0.1%, and unemployment stood at 4.6%.

Services make up 57.7% of output and industry 35.6%, with manufacturing alone at 24.7% of GDP; agriculture accounts for 6.7%. The largest economy in East Asia & Pacific is 4.5 times the size of California, yet income per head sits far down the table: GDP per capita of US$13,862 ranks 78th of 196, and $29,333 international dollars in PPP terms ranks 76th. Government gross debt stands at 98.6% of GDP, according to the IMF. The IMF projects GDP of US$27.08 trillion by 2030, a +39% gain that would leave China 2nd in the IMF ranking.

economies.name: Germany

size_equivalent.label: Larger than any U.S. state (1.2× California)
size_equivalent.name: California

economies.profile:
Germany held 3rd place in the global ranking, but its +7.8% gain in US$ GDP, to US$5.05 trillion, was mostly exchange-rate and price effects, not output: real growth was just +0.2%. The largest economy in Europe & Central Asia, it sits between China (2nd) and Japan (4th) and accounts for 4.27% of world GDP. Services make up 64.5% of output and industry 25.2%, with manufacturing alone at 17.6% and agriculture at 0.9%. Inflation stood at 2.2% and unemployment at 3.7%, while government gross debt reached 62.7% of GDP.

The scale stands out even by American yardsticks: Germany's economy is larger than any U.S. state, at 1.2 times California. GDP per capita came to US$60,496, 18th of 196. Germany also ranked 3rd in 2000, and its US$ GDP has grown 2.6 times since then, from US$1.97 trillion. The IMF projects US$6.15 trillion by 2030, a +22% rise that would keep it 3rd.

economies.name: Japan

size_equivalent.label: About the size of California (2025 GDP)
size_equivalent.name: California

economies.profile:
Japan's economy is smaller in dollar terms than it was at the turn of the century. GDP stood at US$5.04 trillion in 2000, peaked at US$6.33 trillion in 2012 and reached US$4.44 trillion in 2025, a multiple of 0.9x. Japan still ranks 4th of 196, unchanged from 2024, between Germany and the United Kingdom, down from 2nd in 2000. It remains the 2nd largest of 32 economies in East Asia & Pacific, about the size of California.

US$ GDP rose 5.9% in 2025 against real growth of +1.2%. Services account for 71.4% of output and industry 26.8%, with manufacturing at 18.8% and agriculture at 1.0%, all as of 2024. Inflation ran at 3.2% and unemployment at 2.5%, while government gross debt stands at 204.8% of GDP. Output per person is US$35,951, 39th worldwide. The IMF projects GDP of US$4.88 trillion by 2030, up 10%, a level that would rank 6th among economies with forecasts.

economies.name: United Kingdom

size_equivalent.name: California

economies.profile:
The United Kingdom climbed 1 place to 5th in the world, though the dollar gain behind it was mostly exchange-rate and price effects rather than output. US$ GDP rose 8.3% to US$4.00 trillion, while real growth ran at +1.4%. That leaves the British economy sitting between Japan, 4th, and India, 6th, and about the size of California.

Services generate 73.1% of output, industry 16.5% and agriculture 0.6%, with manufacturing at 7.7%. Inflation stood at 3.9% and unemployment at 4.8%, while government gross debt reached 102.1% of GDP. GDP per capita of US$57,602 ranks 20th, but the PPP measure slips to 30th. The long view shows a lower ranking: the UK stood 4th in 2000, when its economy measured US$1.67 trillion, and has grown 2.4 times in dollar terms since. The IMF projects GDP of US$5.18 trillion by 2030, a +29% rise that would keep it 5th.

size_equivalent.name: California

economies.profile:
India's economy expanded 7.6% in real terms in 2025, yet it slipped 1 place to 6th, now behind the United Kingdom and ahead of France. US$ GDP rose 5.2% to US$3.96 trillion, about the size of California. Services make up 49.3% of output, industry 25.2% and agriculture 16.2%, with manufacturing at 13.5%. With 1.46 billion people, GDP per capita was US$2,702, 151st of 196; on a purchasing-power basis it ranks 20 places higher, at 131st, as local prices are low. Inflation ran at 2.4% and government gross debt at 84.3% of GDP.

The longer arc is steeper. India ranked 13th in 2000, when GDP was US$468.4 billion, and output has grown 8.4 times in US$ terms since. The IMF projects GDP of US$6.13 trillion by 2030, a 55% rise that would lift it to 4th.

Services make up 70.9% of output and industry 16.8%, with manufacturing at 9.5% of GDP and agriculture at 1.4%. Inflation was 0.9% and unemployment 7.5%. Government gross debt stands at 115.5% of GDP, according to the IMF.

The longer view shows slippage: France ranked 5th in 2000, and its GDP has grown 2.5 times since then, from US$1.36 trillion. GDP per capita of US$48,986 ranks 27th of 196, but France falls to 32nd on a PPP basis, at $63,975 international dollars. The IMF projects GDP of US$3.97 trillion by 2030, up 18%, which would keep France 7th.

The longer view is modest: GDP has grown 2.2x since 2000, when it stood at US$1.15 trillion and ranked 7th. The IMF projects US$2.96 trillion by 2030, a rise of +16% that would place Italy 10th among economies with forecasts.

The forecast is the striking part. The IMF projects GDP of US$2.65 trillion by 2030, a rise of +45% that would lift Mexico to 12th among economies with forecasts. That would bring it back near the 9th place it held in 2000, when GDP was US$742.1 billion.

The 4th-largest economy in East Asia & Pacific is about the size of Florida. The IMF projects GDP of US$2.49 trillion by 2030, a +38% rise that would lift it to 14th.

Services account for 65.3% of output and agriculture 24.2%, while industry makes up 5.3% and manufacturing 0.5%. Inflation was 2.8% and government gross debt 8.8% of GDP. With a population of 113,683, the economy is smaller than any U.S. metro area, at 20% of Eagle Pass, TX. Micronesia ranked 187th in 2000, when GDP was US$230 million, and output has grown 2.2 times in US$ terms since. The IMF projects GDP of US$616 million by 2030, up 23%, which would place it 183rd.

Kiribati's government gross debt is just 8.0% of GDP, according to the IMF. The economy itself is tiny, at US$349 million in 2025, smaller than any U.S. metro area at 14% of Eagle Pass, TX.

Real growth was +4.2%, ahead of the +1.8% rise in US$ GDP, and Kiribati held 192nd place, between Micronesia and Palau. Inflation was 6.5%. Unemployment for 2025 is not reported.

Services made up 70.3% of output, agriculture 23.2% and industry 11.8% as of 2024, with manufacturing at 4.2% of GDP. With a population of 136,488, GDP per capita is US$2,559, 154th of 196. Local prices are high, so in PPP terms it falls to $3,937 international dollars, 172nd, or 18 places lower.

The economy is 4.7 times its 2000 size of US$75 million, when it also ranked 192nd. The IMF projects GDP of US$465 million by 2030, up 33%, which would place Kiribati 184th. Tarawa is the capital.

economies.profile:
Palau ranks 193rd of 196 by GDP, yet its 17,663 residents earn GDP per capita of US$19,532, 64th in the world. High local prices cut that sharply on a PPP basis: at $23,052 international dollars it ranks 89th, 25 places lower. Real output grew 6.3% and US$ GDP rose 7.3% to US$345 million, holding Palau between Kiribati and the Marshall Islands.

As of 2024, services made up 73.1% of output, industry 13.0%, agriculture 2.7% and manufacturing 1.2%. Consumer prices edged down, with inflation at -0.4%, and government gross debt stood at 52.8% of GDP. The economy is smaller than any U.S. metro area, at 14% of Eagle Pass, TX. In 2000, GDP stood at US$150 million and Palau ranked 189th; US$ GDP has since grown 2.3 times. The IMF projects a +31% rise to US$452 million by 2030, which would place it 185th.

economies.profile:
The Marshall Islands' living standards look far weaker once prices are counted. Output per person is US$8,489, 95th of 196, but on a purchasing-power basis it falls to $8,964 international dollars, 141st, a 46-place drop that reflects high local prices.

At US$308 million, the economy ranks 194th, unchanged, between Palau and Nauru, and is smaller than any U.S. metro area, at 12% of Eagle Pass, TX. US$ GDP rose 8.1% in 2025 against real growth of +2.3%; the 5.8-percentage-point gap was mostly exchange-rate and price effects, not output.

Services account for 68.2% of output, agriculture 19.9% and industry 13.4%, with manufacturing at 3.2%, all as of 2024. Inflation was 4.1% and government gross debt 8.8% of GDP. With a population of 36,282, GDP has grown 2.7x since 2000, when it stood at US$115 million and ranked 190th of 194. The IMF projects US$418 million by 2030, a rise of +36% that would place the islands 186th among economies with forecasts.

Nauru sits next to last in the ranking, at 195th of 196, with GDP of US$176 million and a population of 12,025. Only Tuvalu is smaller; the Marshall Islands sit just above.

Per person the picture shifts. GDP per capita of US$14,640 ranks 75th in the world, but Nauru drops 45 places to 120th on a PPP basis because local prices are high. US$ GDP rose 4.9% in 2025 from US$168 million, with real growth of +2.1%, though it remains below the 2022 peak of US$181 million. Inflation stood at 6.1%, and government gross debt is 12.2% of GDP.

The dollar economy has grown 6.5 times since 2000, when it measured US$27 million and ranked 193rd. It is smaller than any U.S. metro area, at 7% of the size of Eagle Pass, TX. The IMF projects GDP of US$244 million by 2030, a +39% rise, with a forecast ranking of 187th.

Tuvalu is the smallest economy in this edition, ranking 196th of 196 with GDP of US$57 million in 2025, and it held last place in 2000 too, at 194th of 194. Its 9,492 people produced GDP per capita of US$6,041, 115th of 196, though it falls 36 places to 151st on a purchasing-power basis, as local prices are high.

Real growth was 1.6% and US$ GDP rose 1.0%, with output still below its 2021 peak of US$62 million. As of 2015, agriculture made up 15.9% of output and industry 7.0%; manufacturing stood at 1.0% as of 2011. Inflation was 2.9% and government gross debt 2.8% of GDP. Output has grown 3.9 times in US$ terms since 2000, when it was US$15 million. The economy is smaller than any U.S. metro area, at 2% of Eagle Pass, TX. The IMF projects GDP of US$99 million by 2030, a 73% increase that would leave it 188th, last among economies with forecasts.
